Priority Therapeutic Domain 1: Neurotransmission, Neural Circuit Function, and Neuropsychopharmacology
Current prescribing is clinically important but unevenly supported
Medication safety and polypharmacy are implementation-ready priorities
Outcomes must measure function, not only symptom reduction
Initiative 2: Medication Safety and Real-World Outcomes Module
Initiative 3: Biomarker-Informed Neural-Circuit and Adaptive Trial Program
Initiative 4: Functional Augmentation of Communication and Participation
Priority Therapeutic Domain 2: Immune, Autoimmune, and Inflammatory Biology
Established immune and neuroimmune conditions require standard medical care
Prenatal and maternal immune biology is promising but requires causal and safety sequencing
Postnatal immune phenotypes define subgroups, not a universal mechanism
Neuroinflammation and glial biology remain translationally relevant but context-dependent
Recovery, resilience, and fever-responsive change deserve direct study
Initiative 2.2: Acute Neuroimmune Destabilization Evaluation Pathway
Initiative 2.3: Immune Biomarker Harmonization, Validation, and Qualification
Priority Therapeutic Domain 3: Folate Metabolism and One-Carbon Biology
The regulatory record, and the Committee’s position on it.
Three populations must remain distinct to determine whether outcomes are cohort dependent.
Cerebral folate transport is the near-term translational use case
Folate receptor alpha autoantibody testing requires harmonization before implementation
Leucovorin evidence should be advanced through biomarker-defined confirmation
Binding and blocking autoantibodies may help predict response but need prospective validation
Broader one-carbon, methylation, and cofactor strategies remain earlier stage
Initiative 3.1: Folate Receptor Alpha Autoantibody Assay Harmonization
Initiative 3.2: Confirmatory Multicenter Leucovorin Trial in Biomarker-Defined Subgroups
Initiative 3.3: Cerebral Folate Deficiency Recognition, Referral, and Clinical Guidance
Initiative 3.4: One-Carbon, Methylation, and Redox Stratification Studies
Initiative 3.5: NLRP3 Inflammasome as a Cross-Domain One-Carbon/Immune Stratification Target
Priority Therapeutic Domain 4: Gastrointestinal Biology, Microbiome Function, and Nutrition
Gastrointestinal symptoms can present as behavior, sleep disruption, or functional loss
Standard gastrointestinal and nutrition care is ready for implementation now
Microbiome and mucosal findings justify targeted research, not broad clinical adoption
FMT, digestive enzymes, and diet-responsive interventions require evidence-matched sequencing
Initiative 4.1: Standard-of-Care GI Recognition, Pain Assessment, and Nutrition Access
Initiative 4.2: GI Symptom, Pain, and Post-Meal Flare Measurement
Initiative 4.3: Integrated Microbiome, Metabolite, Mucosal, Enzyme, and Diet Biomarker Program
Initiative 4.4: Controlled Precision Trials and Evidence Reviews
Priority Therapeutic Domain 5: Neurodevelopmental Regression, Functional Trajectory, and Health Stabilization
Regression is clinically recognizable but inconsistently acted upon
A subset of regression has identifiable and treatable contributors
Undefined regression requires a common care and research language
Functional trajectory and stabilization must be measured directly
Initiative 5.1: National Regression Recognition and Indicated Diagnostic Pathway
Initiative 5.2: Regression Follow-Up and Health Stabilization Quality Program
Initiative 5.3: NDR-Aligned Biomarker-Defined Functional-Trajectory and Stabilization Studies
Priority Therapeutic Domain 6: Mitochondrial, Redox, Metabolic Function, and Endocrine Biology
Primary mitochondrial disease and secondary dysfunction require different responses
Redox biology is a candidate stratification system, not a treatment indication by itself
Supportive interventions need subgroup evidence and safety monitoring
Emerging metabolic therapies require sequencing before broad testing
Priority 1: National Metabolic and Redox Biomarker Harmonization
Priority 2: Access to Standard Metabolic Evaluation and Emergency Planning
Priority 3: Biomarker-Defined Trials of Mitochondrial and Redox Support
Priority 5: Comparative-Effectiveness and Evidence Threshold Review
Priority 6: Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Health, Measurement, and Longitudinal Research
Autonomic symptoms can be clinically significant
Physiologic measures are promising but not yet harmonized
Wearable and remote measures need clinical-utility guardrails
Autonomic dysregulation interacts with other domains
Intervention endpoints should match the physiology being treated
Priority 1: Clinical Recognition and Standard Care for Dysautonomia
Priority 3: Wearable and Remote Physiology Validation
Priority 4: Pragmatic Trials of Autonomic-Directed Care
Priority 5: Autonomic Physiology Across Sleep, GI, Pain, Sensory, Medication, and Illness Contexts
Priority Therapeutic Domain 8: Sleep and Circadian Regulation
Sleep disturbance is common, consequential, and treatable
Behavioral sleep care and melatonin are ready for wider implementation
Medical contributors must be actively evaluated
Objective sleep and circadian measures should support care and trials
Pharmacologic use requires stronger pediatric safety and durability evidence
Priority 8.1: National Sleep Recognition and Standard Care Implementation
Priority 8.2: Comparative-Effectiveness Review and Sequencing Trials
Priority 8.3: Objective Sleep Measurement and Limited-Communication Assessment
Priority 8.4: Circadian Biology, Melatonin, and Pediatric Safety Monitoring
Priority Therapeutic Domain 9: Epilepsy and Network Excitability
Seizure recognition is harder when communication is limited
Sleep EEG is clinically important in selected presentations
Language loss and ESES/CSWS require specific attention
Network excitability is a plausible mechanism, but not a clinical shortcut
Regression and epilepsy overlap in clinically important subgroups
Safety counseling and SUDEP prevention require adaptation
Priority 1: Epilepsy Recognition and Access Initiative
Priority 2: EEG and Sleep EEG Care Pathways for Selected Presentations
Priority 3: Subclinical Epileptiform Activity and ESES/CSWS Clinical Utility Program
Priority 4: Network Excitability and Biologic Context Studies
Priority 5: Seizure Management and Functional-Trajectory Trials
Priority 6: SUDEP, Safety, and Family-Centered Epilepsy Education
Priority Therapeutic Domain 10: Motor Planning, Praxis, Sensorimotor Integration, and Apraxia
Motor planning is a functional access issue
Differential assessment is essential Speech-motor impairment is likely a major and under-recognized contributor to limited speech
Praxis, dyspraxia and sensorimotor function are measurable but not routinely assessed
Motor access affects research inclusion and assessment validity
Priority 1: Functional Access and Clinically Indicated Services
Priority 2: Differential Assessment and Referral Pathways
Priority 3: Standardized Motor Phenotyping and Measurement Validation

Priority 5: Inclusive Research Design and Assessment Bias Reduction

No approved treatments for core symptoms
Conventional all-comers trials are a poor fit
Off-label use has outpaced the evidence
